strings.text: Road's watched. You're welcome.
Heh. Alright, alright - I like you. You've got the look of someone who buys a guy a drink after. We're good, you and me. Best guardsman in Liscor says so.
A Drake built like a barracks door, spear worn smooth from use, standing at ease the way only dangerous people stand. He watches the road and everyone on it. Including you, now.
Straw and burlap lashed to posts, hacked half to ribbons. Someone drills here often, and hard. The stitching tells you where a real guard would break.
Relc whistles. "Not bad for a start. Now go SLEEP on it — Classes come at the pillow, not the podium. Bed's upstairs at the inn."
A cairn on a hill. The view is mostly weather.
[Eagle Eyes] — The plains resolve: the gate road, the ruin east past it, and every fold of dead ground a warband could hide in. You'll walk this land differently now.
From up here the floodplains pretend to be a map. Good eyes could read it.
The seam splits wider at your touch, cold air breathing out of the dark beneath. You step through, into somewhere else.
A hairline crack runs through old, dressed stone half-swallowed by turf — not natural rock, something built. Cold air breathes up out of it, and it smells of somewhere else.
A cold seam splits the earth here, sealed by old stone. It doesn't feel like it goes anywhere. Yet.
Three boulders sit too evenly spaced for the hillside's own tumble, and one of them, you'd swear, just shifted.
The crab regards you with all the tameable warmth of a boulder.
Nothing moving out there. Whatever it was keeps day hours, same as everyone sane.
A patrol slipping the boulder line, quiet until they're not. Only after dark.
A shape stands too still at the treeline, antlers catching a warmth that isn't sunlight.
A scrape of trampled grass, two long-beaked shapes hunched low over it, watching you watch them.

A corusdeer, down in the grass with a leg it won't put weight on. Its antlers barely glow. It watches you the way anything hurt watches anything larger. It would let patient hands close, and hands that tend enough hurt beasts learn something no drill yard teaches.
[Beast's Mending] — Splint and salve, and the leg sits straighter than it has any right to. The corusdeer breathes easier.
[Beast's Mending] — The splint comes away and stays away. It stands, tests the leg, and goes to find the herd. Your hands knew what to do because of this deer.
It has let you close once today. Don't spend what little trust it has.
You move slow, keep your hands low, and it lets you check the leg. That, from a wild thing, is everything.
It knows you now. It holds still while you work, and its antlers warm the air between you.
It is already standing when you come. It lets you run a hand down the leg once, then turns and goes up the rise at a trot, and does not look back.
A body-shaped hollow pressed into the grass, going green again at the edges. Something lay here a long time, and then stopped needing to.
In the flattened grass, shed clean at the base: one antler, oaken-brown fading to a red glow at the tip. It is warm to hold, and stays warm.
Only the hollow in the grass now, and it is filling in.
The pup sniffs your hand once, twice — then leans its whole small weight against your leg. That's that, then.
The pup shrinks back. You don't have the hands for this yet — hands like that are learned on hurt animals, one at a time. There's a corusdeer down in the grass east of here that would let you start.
A scrape under the boulder line, and in it one wolf pup, ribs showing, too young to be alone. The pack that left it is not coming back.
It watches your hands. Whatever you mean to offer it, offer it properly.
It bites you exactly once, decides you took it well, and climbs your sleeve to glare at the horizon from a better vantage.
It snaps at your fingers. Fair enough. Nothing wild takes an offer from hands that have never tended anything.
A razorbeak chick, blown or chased from the nest scrape, hissing at the whole world from behind a tussock. The nest is close. The parents are not.
It stops hissing when you crouch. Interested, then — if you make the offer the right way.
It walks out of the scrape without being asked and stands on your foot. The pack keeps its own counsel about who leaves with whom.
The pup watches you the way it watches weather. Hands that can take an offer like this are learned on hurt animals, one at a time.
The scrape under the boulder line has been dug out again and re-lined. A season on, and there is a pup in it: bolder than the last one, and entirely unimpressed by you.
It has not learned to be afraid of hands yet. Make the offer before it does.
It stalks the length of your arm, finds the shoulder acceptable, and settles there facing backwards. Somebody has to watch the way you came.
It flares its hackles and holds the tussock. Nothing wild takes an offer from hands that have never tended anything.
The nest scrape has fledged another. This one has already worked out that the tussock is cover and that you are not, and it is holding both facts against you.
It goes still when you crouch, which from a razorbeak is an invitation. Make the offer properly.
It leans, the way the first one leaned. You are not being given a replacement. You are being given another one.
The pup does not move. Hands that can take an offer like this are learned on hurt animals, one at a time.
Late in the season and thin with it, but another scrape further down the boulder line is occupied. Whatever else the floodplains do, they keep doing this.
It is too tired to flinch. Offer, and mean it.
The small figure on the rise watches you. It does not move to meet you.
A small figure on the rise south, standing very still. It has been watching you for a while, and it wants you to know that.
You go down between the stones sideways, the way the flattened grass says to, and the plains close over the top of you.
Two low stones lean together where the ground folds away, and the grass between them is beaten flat by small feet. Smoke comes up thin and does not spread.
The road's empty in the daylight. Whatever works this verge keeps to the dark.
Two heavy shapes working the verge of the wagon road, wings folded tight, close enough to the carter camps to smell the fires. Only after dark.
A scatter of old bones the wolf will not leave alone. It noses through them, circles, noses again, and looks back at you as though the next part is your job.
You dig where the wolf keeps insisting. Under the bones, wrapped in rotted cloth: a charm on a cord gone soft with age.
Turned bones and nothing under them now. The wolf has lost interest, which is its own verdict.
A boulder standing clear of the reeds with the whole pond below it. The razorbeak keeps climbing it and screaming at the water, which is either an opinion or a report.

It wheels out over the pond, hangs, and comes back loud. There is something square and man-made on the bottom, a stride out from the bank — too far to reach across open water, and water can be made to bear weight.
The meat is good and it will not stay good. Raw and cold, it is no use to you, and you have no way to change that.

A young corusdeer down in the grass with its neck wrong, cold hours ago and not yet found by anything with teeth. The hide is whole. The haunches are worth carrying, if you had a way to make them keep.
[Flame Jet] — You run the lance along the haunch until the fat goes loud and the outside blackens. You cut what will travel and leave the rest to the grass.
Hauling at it with your hands gets you nothing. Fire is what this wants.
The paint is newer than the post it hangs on. Somebody meant it, and means it still.
A hand-painted board, letters gone bold where they were traced twice: THE WANDERING INN — NO KILLING GOBLINS.
Whatever's under there won't come to bare hands. Lism's shelf had a fisher's handline.

The pond narrows here over a drop the light doesn't reach. Every so often the water moves wrong, and then it stops, the way a room stops when you walk into it. Whatever keeps this water is not interested in being caught.
The water's gone still. Whatever considered you today is done considering.
You pay out the line into the dark water. Nothing takes it, and nothing was ever going to — whatever keeps this pool knows the difference between an offer and a hook.

Something square and man-made rests on the pond floor a stride out from the bank, furred with silt. Too far to reach across open water. But water can be made to bear weight, if you know the trick of cold.

Kneeling on the ice, you lever the silt-caked strongbox free. Drake-work, old, its lock long rusted through. Inside, dry against all odds, a few keepsakes someone drowned here meant never to be found.
The strongbox sits open and empty now, holding nothing but pond-light.
Scree slides out from under your boot and rattles away down the slope. Getting up that needs surer feet than yours.

A ring of river stones with a fire kept deliberately small. Someone has banked it low and swept the ash back, so the smoke goes up thin instead of out wide. Nothing about this fire wants to be seen from the road.
The wood is sorted by burn time in three piles. Somebody in this camp thinks two nights ahead.
Green hides pegged out on a lattice of spear-shafts, scraped down to nothing on one side. The pegs are all different lengths, whittled to fit whatever the rack needed that day.
Every hide is stretched to the same tension. Whoever runs this rack does not let anyone else near it.
A flat stone at the high end of the hollow, worn smooth in one small patch. It faces the way in. There is no cushion, no cover, and nothing near enough to hide behind.
From here you can see the cut in the turf, the fire, and everyone's hands at once. It was not chosen for comfort.
A shoulder yoke cut for someone half your height, propped against a stack of empty baskets. The baskets go out full and come back full of something else.
The baskets are all out. Nothing left to haul until they come back.
You shorten the yoke by two notches and spend the morning hauling water and cut brush. Somebody presses coin into your hand at the end without looking up.
The yoke has been left out on your side of the fire. Nobody says anything about it, and nobody moves it back.
A goblin sitting where the light from the cut in the turf lands, sharpening something that is already sharp. It has not looked directly at you once.
A rack of split poles standing empty over a bed of ash. The hunters look north at the range, and then back at it, and say nothing.
The poles are bare and the ash is cold. Hands on the camp's baskets first, the old one signs at you, and then something big brought down off the range north.
You hang what you brought back and cut it down thin the way the old one shows you, and by the time the light goes the rack is heavy for the first time this year.
The poles are bowed under strips cut thin and even, and the ash beneath has been banked warm to hold the smoke in them.
Nobody moves the rack aside when you pass it now.
Three of them stand on the lip of the hollow where it is easiest to come down, looking at the racks and doing arithmetic. Nobody in the camp is pretending not to have noticed.
